# Commission: The software house becomes its own client

## Intended contribution

Write a genuinely fresh, self-contained, short lead article for technical readers with no KB context. One empirical bet, then two conditional arguments. A software house that improves a client's program has a development capability. If it uses that capability to search for, judge, install and retain changes to how it does its own next job, it has a learning loop. The empirical bet is that LLMs can do the needed selection, as well as helping search, well enough that later work improves without per-edit human judgment. Fully automated search and selection may scale with compute; a stronger research-like design may yield sample efficiency and bounded explanations. Build the narrative around that distinction, not around classification or an abstract value-function argument.

## Must keep

Use one explicitly hypothetical failure: a nominally documentation-only edit actually affects a client's build. Show TWO repairs: diagnose/test/ship the external product fix (not by itself evidence the house learned); then the house becomes its own client. Compare concrete remedies to its test-selection workflow (run all tests, exception for this file, inspect build dependencies, leave unchanged); judge missed failures vs cost, investigate facts, can reject or try a reviewed variant. Show later work on another job causally changed by selected retained method rather than merely citing it. Model weights need not change. Search includes useful candidates and discriminating tests; selection is a real comparison without necessarily a single score, not proof of gain. State how to test downstream gain versus credible baseline over further work including compute/review/rollback costs. External requirements and feedback don't make the choice human-assisted unless people make the internal decisions at issue. Briefly distinguish self-edit of procedures under a fixed criterion from further revision of how it judges future self-edits (double-loop); avoid conflating client product test rule with own criterion for adopting workflow revisions.

Compatibility with Bitter Lesson is conditional on additional computation doing domain-specific discovery and selection instead of a human providing every decisive new diagnosis/test/verdict; unattended scripts alone don't suffice, representation isn't the issue, actual scaling still needs measurement. Stronger design: winning patches suffice for base loop; separately retain and act on revisable hypotheses with predictions, evidence and tests. How that changes the next inquiry. Sample efficiency means fewer new target observations to reach comparable performance under a task shift preserving structure, compared with same model and history but only case records/reconstruction; not necessarily less compute. Explainability is only a bounded claim about an operative rule: intervention with/without it or change the dependency; legibility isn't faithfulness and doesn't explain model internals. End with a mixed result that would support one claim without the others and honest evidence status (no demonstrated end-to-end autonomous Commonplace loop). Link readers to the judgment and empirical-test companions where useful.

## Must exclude

Do not preserve the former architecture, historical tour, comparison table, gallery of pitfalls, decision-analysis tutorial, full experimental protocol or an obligatory further-reading catalogue. No new unsupported historical claims. No claim of gains from a hypothetical. Do not update adjacent notes, infrastructure, index or companions. Write for an external reader; avoid the language of commissions and preserve-lists in the body.

## Reserved decisions

Keep existing title, path, byline, draft status and banner. No additional artifacts. The old article is not a checklist of content to keep. Aim for roughly 1000–1500 words, shorter if the argument is made. Keep source_notes accurate for the fresh text. Report inbound consequences, don't recreate obsolete material for backlinks.

## Current direction

User approved writing from scratch on the self-editing pivot; use selection for the client's software before turning the same capability on the developer's own methods. Bring in reflexivity only after showing it; no technical label needed where plain language works. The question is what closes the learning loop and what further assumptions buy which payoffs. Strong concrete article, not another version of the judgment companion.

# Software house

A **software house** is the complete persistent system responsible for developing and evolving software for external users. It operates in response to their requirements, feedback, and the consequences that arise when the software meets its operating environment. It is not necessarily a company, tool, or particular production method.

The software house includes the software whose evolution it remains responsible for, any production knowledge and machinery it uses, and every person or computational component that fills an internal production role. This functional boundary generalizes ordinary usage, in which a software house is an organization of people and tools. It lets the same term cover human, hybrid, and automated producers without making one role allocation part of the base definition.

## Scope

Users remain outside the software house when they supply requirements, domain knowledge, preferences, feedback, acceptance judgments, or later demands. A person is inside the software house only when the system depends on them for an internal production role, such as interpreting production knowledge, making implementation decisions, or repairing production machinery.

The same person can occupy both positions in different interactions. The boundary follows the role being performed, not the person's identity or legal relationship to an organization.

The house's products and responsibilities can change as requirements develop; it need not declare a product family in advance. Persistence means continuity of responsibility for software evolution across demands and operating consequences. It does not mean indefinite life, immutable membership, or retention of every state change.

Persistence alone establishes neither retention nor learning. It identifies continuity of responsibility, not a causal dependence of later production on a change made from experience. A theoretical software house whose fixed production knowledge and machinery suffice for every admitted demand still meets this definition. Responding to a demand may change the software without changing the house's capacity or production method. Claims that the house retained experience, learned, or revised its production machinery must be derived and tested separately.

An **automated software house** performs every internal production role computationally. User participation is compatible with automation; dependence on a human for an internal production role is not.

An evaluation examines particular work over a particular period. Those limits bound what its evidence establishes; they do not define the house's future responsibilities.

## Exclusions

A company is not the only possible software house, and its legal or organizational boundary need not equal the software house's system boundary. Conversely, a tool, model, agent harness, workflow, or production method is not the whole software house merely because the house uses it.

A [software factory](./software-factory.md), in Greenfield's sense, is family-specific production machinery that a software house may use. It is neither the software house nor a required component of one. Human developers required to operate or revise that machinery are inside the surrounding software house while filling those production roles, even though they are not part of the factory machinery itself. This definition does not import Greenfield's product-family, schema, template, or developer-role ontology.

## Misuse Cases

- Calling an IDE, LLM, agent harness, or generator a software house when it is only one component of the producing system.
- Counting a user as part of the software house merely because their requirements or feedback affect the software.
- Calling a software house automated when a human still performs an internal production role.
- Treating persistence as indefinite existence rather than continued responsibility across software changes.
- Treating persistence as evidence that the house retained experience or learned from it.

# Self-improving system

A **self-improving system** makes operative changes to its own behavior-determining organization, where those changes are causally responsive to evidence bearing on an **improvement objective**.

*Its own* means the object of change is the system's [behavior-determining organization](./behavior-determining-organization.md) — its parameters, policies, memory, rules, workflows, code — not an external work product. A compiler that optimizes programs is not self-improving; a compiler pipeline that rewrites its own optimizer is. This is Ashby's two-loop distinction: operating a system is one loop, modifying the system that operates is another. The attribution is assessed against a declared boundary: a model fine-tuned by an external training pipeline is being improved, while the composite of model plus pipeline self-improves — [the boundary cases make this dependence explicit](../the-self-improving-system-definition-classifies-its-boundary-cases.md).

*Operative* means the change affects subsequent operation over the relevant horizon, through a consumer, a channel, and a force — [operative change](./operative-change.md), which does not require permanence; a transient compensation, or a change nothing ever acts on, does not qualify.

*Makes* is read over a declared assessment horizon, like operativity: a system is self-improving over that horizon when evidence-responsive operative self-change occurs within it. The dispositional attribution — the system *has* a standing improvement pathway, currently exercised or not — is also available, but it is a different claim and must be marked as such; a pathway nothing has exercised over the relevant horizon supports only the dispositional reading. Tense, like boundary, is declared rather than fixed by the definition.

## The causal anatomy

For an occurrent attribution, four causal obligations must close within the declared boundary and horizon:

1. Evidence bearing on the objective causally shapes the determination of an update.
2. The result becomes a change to the bounded system's own behavior-determining organization, rather than remaining evidence, a proposal, or an external work product.
3. The changed organization enters a live behavioral-authority path with a consumer, channel, and force capable of reaching later behavior.
4. A subsequent operation exercises that path and causally depends on the change.

These are logical roles, not required components or stages. A direct update can determine and install its successor in one transition; another architecture can separate proposal, acceptance, and installation. The membership test asks whether the causal dependencies close, not how many components realize them.

Persistence and availability establish less than this path. A saved episode that never affects an updater fails the first obligation. An accepted proposal that never becomes part of the organization fails the second. An installed artifact with no live consumer fails the third. Mandatory loading establishes a channel, but if the consumer ignores the content, the fourth remains unestablished. Storage, retrieval, acceptance, installation, and loading are therefore evidence about particular links, not substitutes for the end-to-end attribution.

## Evidence-responsiveness does not require a gate

*Responsive to evidence* is defined in [evidence bearing on an improvement objective](./evidence-bearing-on-an-improvement-objective.md). There must be a loss, reward, error, viability bound, test, judgment, or other criterion for the evidence to bear on; otherwise the change is merely caused, not improvement-directed.

The evidence may directly determine an update that is always adopted, or it may evaluate a candidate that can be rejected. A separately represented candidate, evaluator, or acceptance gate is therefore not required by membership. The [proposal-selection improvement loop](../a-proposal-selection-loop-requires-search-evaluation-and-retention.md) owns that named subtype and its search, evaluation, oracle, and retention vocabulary.

Update architecture attaches to a named pathway, target aspect, and granularity, not to a whole system. A gradient step may be direct while a checkpoint-release gate around it uses proposal selection, and one system may compose both kinds of pathway.

> An improvement criterion is required semantically; an explicit evaluator is not required architecturally.

## What membership leaves open

Membership establishes improvement-directed self-change, not a complete architecture or a successful outcome. Evidence-responsiveness can faithfully pursue a bad objective, and an evaluator can accept a harmful change: only outcome evidence establishes that improvement occurred.

Classify the remaining questions elsewhere:

- [Reflective system](./reflective-system.md) owns whether the pathway changes itself through a causally connected self-representation; reflection is not required for membership.
- [The pathway profile](../../tags/self-improving-systems-README.md) owns reflective structure, improvement dynamics, governance, and actor allocation; [the cumulativity criterion itself](../accumulation-counts-dependence-through-the-retained-result.md) is held separately.
- [Methodological and computational closure](../methodological-and-computational-closure-track-different-changes.md) owns the two closure readings, and [warranted autonomy](../warranted-autonomy-is-bounded-by-oracle-domain.md) owns when unattended evaluation is trustworthy.

## Exclusions

- **Not self-modification alone.** Blind or accidental rewrites lack evidence-responsiveness.
- **Not regulation alone.** A thermostat changes its environment, not its own behavior-determining organization; a learning thermostat that revises its controller does.
- **Not work-product improvement.** Improving an answer or external code does not change the improving system's own organization.
- **Not reflection, a gate, or autonomy.** Each may describe a member, but none is a membership condition.
- **Not guaranteed success.** The term names an improvement-directed mechanism, not a favorable outcome.

## Misuse Cases

- Treating the proposal-selection improvement loop as the definition rather than a named subtype, which re-smuggles an architecture into semantics.
- Treating stored or retrieved evidence as an operative update without showing that it affects the update determination and results in organizational change.
- Treating acceptance, installation, or loading as proof that a subsequent operation causally depends on the change.
- Reporting an autonomy grade without declaring the boundary it was assessed against.
- Attributing self-improvement without naming the objective it is indexed to, or naming one the pathway's evidence is not diagnostic of — [the first leaves the attribution elliptical, the second makes it false](../self-improvement-is-relative-to-a-declared-objective.md).
- Reading a dormant improvement pathway as current self-improvement — the dispositional claim (*has* a pathway) and the horizon claim (evidence-responsive change is occurring over this horizon) are different attributions.
- Treating a helpful change to an external product as self-improvement of the tool that produced it.

## Provenance

Commonplace treats the predicate as frame-indexed. The bearer of the property is a bounded system — a system under a declared boundary — not a substrate simpliciter, so an attribution is elliptical until the boundary is named. The fine-tuning-pipeline case in [the boundary cases](../the-self-improving-system-definition-classifies-its-boundary-cases.md) shows why: the same substrate is being improved under one boundary and self-improving under another.

Self-representation and reject-capable evaluation are not membership conditions. Reflection instead names a structural property whose distinctive benefit is developed in [reflection buys addressability](../reflection-buys-addressability.md), while proposal selection names the narrower update architecture with a rejectable adoption decision.

This architecture-neutral choice is consistent with uses of “self-improving” for gateless self-tuning algorithms ([Ailon et al. 2011](../../sources/self-improving-algorithms.ingest.md)) and with self-adaptive-systems literature treating feedback-loop models as engineering reference models rather than definitions ([Weyns](../../sources/weyns-software-engineering-self-adaptive-systems-tour.ingest.md); [Petrovska, Erjiage, and Kugele 2025](../../sources/defining-self-adaptive-systems-systematic-literature-review.ingest.md)). It is Commonplace's explication, not a claimed field consensus.

# Selection-based learning

<!-- Maintenance: when changing this definition, please apply the checks in
[selection-based-learning-checks.md](./selection-based-learning-checks.md).
This term was named "deliberative learning" until 2026-11-22 and
"judgment-governed self-improvement" on that day. -->

**Selection-based learning** is learning in which each change is selected:

> A change to what the system retains for its later work is proposed,
> evaluated on whether it makes that work better, and can be rejected.

[AlphaGo Zero](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24270) illustrates the boundary. Each newly trained network played the current best one and replaced it only if it won by a margin of 55%. Its successor, [AlphaZero](../../sources/alphazero-chess-shogi-self-play.ingest.md), dropped that evaluation gate and updated a single network continually by gradient descent—moving from network-level selection to direct updates alone.

That contrast divides learning in [Simon's sense](../learning-is-not-only-about-generality.md)—changes that alter what a system can do on later occasions, rather than one-off plans for the current task—into two modes. In a **direct update**, evidence determines the change directly and nothing is proposed or rejected. In **selection-based learning**, a **selection-based learner** operates through a [proposal-selection improvement loop](../a-proposal-selection-loop-requires-search-evaluation-and-retention.md) with two requirements:

- **Retained change.** The change alters something the learner keeps and draws on in later work. Where that retained content lives does not matter: a handbook, code, a team's working habits, and a model checkpoint all qualify, so a readable store is not required.
- **Reject-capable evaluation.** Evaluation is causally distinct from proposing, though it need not be a separate stage or actor and may be automatic. Its verdict decides whether the change is made—or undone if already made—and rejection is its own event rather than the arrival of the next candidate.

Like reinforcement learning, the term names a process rather than a successful outcome. Whether a selected change actually improved the system is a separate question, answered by comparing the system with and without it.

## Scope

- **Direct updates (outside).** Gradient steps under a fixed loss and rules that write directly from inputs (such as raising an article's rank on each click) try no candidate and reject nothing.
- **Triggers and automatic storage (outside).** A rule written automatically on a count trigger and a logger that saves every trace evaluate nothing. Either enters scope only when an evaluation step checks the candidate and can reject it.
- **One fixed measure (inside).** Keeping a patch that passes a validator, deploying the checkpoint with the best validation score, or keeping a mutation in evolutionary search all evaluate a candidate and can reject it. The gradient steps that produced each checkpoint stay outside.
- **Several measures (inside).** A team or judge that weighs a score alongside other considerations and can reject a change even when the score rises.

## System boundary and class of changes

Every claim of selection-based learning names the **system** that changes and the **class of changes** it covers. A wiki that imports pages automatically and lets editors delete wrong ones is outside for imports and inside for deletions.

Who performs the selection does not affect membership, but it separates three levels. Take a deployed model whose checkpoint is picked by a validation score:

1. **Learning.** Only the deployed model sits inside the boundary; it changes which checkpoint it uses, learning by selection that others perform on it.
2. **Self-improvement by selection.** The selection script sits inside the boundary too; the model and script together form a [self-improving system](./self-improving-system.md).
3. **Double-loop.** The engineers who can revise the validation score also sit inside; the combined system can change what it selects by and is [double-loop](./single-loop-and-double-loop-learning.md).

Proposals may come from outside the boundary; selection is the step that must sit inside for self-improvement by selection.

## Misuse Cases

- Citing the term as evidence that the system improved or corrects itself.
- Restricting the term to readable stores or to prose.
- Applying the term to a system because it reasons carefully about its work; it applies only to how retained changes are decided.
- Omitting the system or the class of changes.

# Single-loop and double-loop learning

A system that learns by a
[proposal-selection improvement loop](../a-proposal-selection-loop-requires-search-evaluation-and-retention.md)
decides each proposed change by a criterion: a single measure, a gate, a
check, a formula, or a comparison across several measures. For a named class of
changes, the learner is **single-loop** when it decides those changes under
a criterion it cannot revise, and **double-loop** when it can revise that
criterion so that a different criterion governs later decisions of that
class. Such a system is a
[selection-based learner](./selection-based-learning.md) that does its own
selecting, and the distinction applies whether its criterion is one measure
or several.

The distinction matters because a single-loop learner cannot recover from a
misleading criterion. It keeps applying the criterion however often changes
that passed it turn out badly.

## Scope

- **Applying or speeding up versus revising.** Dropping an instruction
  because a validator rejects it applies the existing criterion. Making the
  validator run faster checks the same criterion sooner. Revising what the
  validator accepts, because instructions that passed it kept misrouting
  agents, changes the criterion for later instructions.
- **Several measures.** A learner that compares across several measures
  can count a new one in any single decision. It is
  double-loop only when a change
  in what counts, or how much, is retained and governs later decisions of
  that class. A team deciding that context cost now counts against every
  routing rule is an example. A team that happens to mention context cost
  in one decision is not.
- **Scoped to one class.** A team paired with a link repairer is double-loop
  for *link repairs* when it can revise the repairer's validator. Whether it
  can also revise how it judges *validator edits* is a separate question.
- **Depends on the named system.**
  [PRODIGY](../../sources/minton-utility-of-ebl-aaai88.ingest.md) alone was
  single-loop: it kept or dropped rules by a utility formula it could not
  change. PRODIGY together with Minton, who chose and revised that formula,
  was double-loop.

A claim of double-loop capacity says what can bring the criterion into
question, what considers it, and what change to the criterion can follow.

## Exclusions

- **Nested loops.** A hyperparameter search wrapped around a training run
  has two nested loops and stays single-loop if one fixed validation score
  governs every pick.
- **A different verdict under the same criterion.** In
  [EURISKO](../../sources/eurisko-learns-new-heuristics-and-domain-concepts.ingest.md),
  dropping one badly generalized heuristic changes one item and is
  single-loop. Retaining a restriction that penalizes future generalizations
  of that shape before they run revises the criterion and is double-loop.
- **A successor that ranks nothing differently.** In
  [Schmidhuber's Gödel machine](../../sources/goedel-machines-schmidhuber.ingest.md),
  proving under the current utility function that a successor utility
  function should be installed is double-loop only when that successor ranks
  later alternatives differently.
- **Argyris's full sense.** The terms are borrowed from
  [Argyris](../../sources/argyris-organizational-learning-and-mis-1977.ingest.md)
  and used more narrowly. In his account, single-loop learning corrects
  errors while "the underlying program is not questioned", and double-loop
  learning questions "the underlying objectives and policies". Here
  double-loop requires only that the working criterion can be revised. A
  learner can keep its declared objective fixed while revising the gates and
  validators that serve it, because
  [revising the objective itself needs a licence from outside it](../revising-an-improvement-objective-is-licensed-from-outside-it.md).

## Misuse Cases

- Using either term without naming the class of changes.
- Reading *double-loop* in Argyris's full sense, as questioning the terminal
  objective.
- Calling a learner double-loop because it has two loops, or because it
  reversed one earlier decision.
- Calling a system double-loop when the criterion is revised only by people
  outside the named system.

# Can an LLM Judge Which Changes Are Worth Making?

> **Draft.** The claims and structure of this article may change. Comments
> and counterexamples are welcome on
> [the repository's GitHub Discussions page](https://github.com/zby/commonplace/discussions).

In open-ended work—maintaining a software repository, curating an internal
knowledge base, or revising a company's refund policy—someone repeatedly
faces a concrete choice: keep the current setup, adopt a proposed change,
or try a narrower version of it. No single score settles every such choice,
because gains and losses fall on different tasks and different people. Yet
maintainers make these calls every day without inventing a global formula.

This article states an **empirical conjecture**, not a new definition of
improvement: **given a stated purpose, real alternatives, and a way to
obtain relevant evidence, a large language model (LLM) may be able to judge
which change is worth making for the work ahead.** The model need not find
the best conceivable change or be right on every proposal. To be useful,
its selections only have to beat a credible baseline—such as a project's
existing admission check—over a stream of real work, once investigation
cost, human help, and mistakes before rollback are counted.

To keep that claim testable, we adopt
[strict necessary preference](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)
as our working definition of improvement. Once the alternative, the work,
the affected parties, and the horizon are fixed, a change counts as an
**improvement** when every way of weighing the consequences compatible with
the stated purpose favors it over the alternative. When every compatible
weighting favors the current state, the change is a **loss**; when
compatible weightings pull in opposite directions or decisive facts are
missing, the comparison stays **open**. That working definition is fixed
before testing, not presented as the only meaning of *better*—and it does
not forbid acting when a comparison is open.

Three observations make the LLM conjecture worth testing rather than
dismissing on sight. First,
[selection needs only a local comparison](../theory/selection-based-learning-needs-only-a-local-comparison.md):
because proposing changes is costly, a judge never has to rank every
possible version of a system—only the candidate at hand against the current
state or a few nearby alternatives. Second, many decisive facts already
live in readable records—error logs, issue trackers, configuration files,
policy documents, and test suites—that an LLM can read or query. Third,
under necessary preference, a judge does not have to invent arbitrary
weights for genuine value conflicts; it only needs to settle clear cases
and expose the missing fact or unstated commitment when a comparison stays
open.

Most of this article uses a software-maintenance example, not because
software development is the only domain where this applies, but because
software teams already keep unusually clear records—diffs, changelogs,
tests, and support matrices—that make it easy to see where each piece of
evidence comes from. The same structure appears wherever work is guided by
retained rules or procedures, from editing an operational handbook to
deciding who may approve customer refunds.

## Inside one decision

Take a constructed example. An automated maintenance agent opens a pull
request upgrading a project's parser dependency from version 2.4 to 3.0.
The changelog says version 3.0 fixes a bug that causes malformed timestamp
fields to fail parsing, and drops support for Python 3.9. The project's
continuous-integration (CI) suite runs on Python 3.12 and passes.

Notice what those two artifacts—the changelog and a green CI run—do **not**
tell a judge:

1. **Whether the fix matters to this project.** Does the project ever
   receive inputs that trigger the malformed-timestamp bug? An upstream fix
   that never touches this project's data buys nothing here.
2. **Whether the removed runtime is a live commitment.** Does the project
   promise Python 3.9 compatibility in its packaging metadata, release
   policy, or customer contracts—and do real deployments still run on it?

A naive judge reading only the pull request sees a bug fix and green tests,
and merges. A slightly more cautious judge sees *"drops Python 3.9"* and
rejects. Neither has checked the facts that actually decide the case.

Follow what happens when a judge treats *"what would count as better work
here, and how could we tell?"*
([defining improvement for open-ended work](../theory/defining-improvement-for-open-ended-work.md))
as an investigative step rather than a guess. Under our working definition,
four different factual situations on the exact same pull request produce
four distinct verdicts and reasonable decisions:

- **Live bug, retired runtime (*improvement*).** Production error logs show
  recurring failures matching the malformed-timestamp bug; replaying one
  captured input confirms version 2.4 rejects it while version 3.0 parses
  it and produces the expected downstream output; packaging metadata and
  deployment configs show the project dropped Python 3.9 six months ago.
  Every compatible way of weighing the project's work favors merging: a
  live failure is fixed and no commitment is broken.
- **Unreached bug, active commitment (*loss*).** Searching six months of
  error logs and input schemas shows the project never passes timestamps
  through that code path, while `pyproject.toml` and the support policy
  still promise Python 3.9 through the end of the year. Breaking a standing
  commitment for zero local benefit loses under every compatible weighting,
  so rejecting is straightforward.
- **Live bug and active commitment (*open for trade-off disagreement*).**
  Captured production inputs hit the bug *and* active customers still
  deploy on Python 3.9. Compatible weightings now pull in opposite
  directions, and counting more bug reports will not settle whose loss
  takes priority. A capable judge should neither merge silently nor reject
  blindly: it can look for a different alternative (such as a narrow
  input-sanitizing workaround that keeps Python 3.9 working), or leave the
  comparison open and escalate the exact conflict to a maintainer.
- **Incomplete records (*open for missing evidence*).** Telemetry covers
  only the company's hosted service, not self-hosted installations, and
  shows zero Python 3.9 runs. **An observed absence in incomplete logs is
  not proof of no affected users.** Because a plausible answer—active
  self-hosted deployments on Python 3.9—would reverse a merge decision, the
  comparison stays open for missing evidence rather than clearing the
  upgrade.

Nothing about that four-way fork is unique to code. Consider a constructed
operational example: a branch manager proposes letting counter staff
approve routine refunds under $50 without head-office sign-off. The
proposal text alone tells a judge neither how long customers currently wait
for head-office checks nor how often branch records miss prior disputes. If
store logs track completed refunds but never record customers who walked
out while waiting—or never tie later chargebacks back to specific branch
approvals—an empty error column again leaves the comparison open for
missing evidence rather than proving safety. Whether the domain is a parser
upgrade, a refund rule, or a knowledge base, the hard part of the judgment
is locating which missing fact could reverse the verdict and knowing when
the available records cannot supply it.

## Where the evidence comes from

Saying *"an LLM judges the change"* leaves the surrounding machinery
unspecified. Two plausible designs—and a hybrid between them—divide the
work differently between the model and the system around it.

| Arrangement | What the model receives | What the model must supply | What stays outside the model |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Evidence packet** | A prepared bundle: proposed diff, stated commitments, relevant logs or test runs, their provenance, and known coverage gaps | Weighing the supplied evidence against the purpose, spotting missing facts or conflicts, and returning a verdict or escalation | Deciding which records to pull, which tests to run, and which commitments to surface |
| **Tool-using investigator** | The proposal, the stated purpose, and read/query/test/ask tools under a budget | Choosing which question could reverse the verdict, running checks, respecting coverage limits, using the answer, and stopping when inquiry stops paying off | Tool definitions, permissions, budget limits, and the records themselves |

The boundary between these two setups matters when evaluating the bet.

**Packet curation is already judgment.** If a human engineer—or a
domain-specific script written for this exact failure mode—selects the one
log query that surfaces the malformed-timestamp errors and pastes the exact
runtime-support clause into the prompt, much of the hardest diagnostic work
has already been done before the LLM runs. Calling the resulting merge
decision *"autonomous LLM judgment"* misattributes the curator's work to
the model. An honest packet-based test must record who chose the packet's
contents and treat the packet builder as part of the system being assessed.

**Tools do not by themselves confer judgment.** Giving an LLM access to a
repository, log queries, a test runner, and a messaging channel to ask
maintainers does not mean it will use them well. To earn its keep in a
tool-using loop, the judge has to clear four bars:

1. *Investigate only what could reverse the verdict.* As
   [necessary preference](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md#open-for-missing-evidence-open-for-trade-offs)
   notes, an unknown is worth checking only if a plausible answer could flip
   the choice. Running a generic linter or re-running an already-green
   Python 3.12 test suite spends budget on answers that cannot change the
   decision.
2. *Read coverage limits alongside results.* Knowing that hosted telemetry
   excludes self-hosted users is what prevents treating zero observed runs
   as zero affected users.
3. *Let the answer move the verdict.* An LLM can run a tool, cite its
   output in plausible prose, and still stick to its initial bias—the same
   gap between plausible prose and causal grounding noted in
   [rationale faithfulness](../theory/revision-guided-by-rationale-needs-faithfulness-not-just-legibility.md).
4. *Stop when further inquiry is not worth its cost.* Exhaustive auditing
   of a trivial, easily reversible change wastes more effort than the
   change could ever save; conversely, when no record settles whose loss
   takes priority, asking a maintainer for a commitment or leaving the
   comparison open is the right place to stop.

In practice, a **hybrid** arrangement is often the most sensible starting
point: a fixed, lightweight packet supplies cheap standing context (the
diff, declared support policies, CI status, and known telemetry gaps),
while bounded tools let the model run targeted checks—like replaying a
captured failing input against the candidate dependency—and escalate when
it hits an unrecorded commitment.

## Testing the bet without asking the judge to grade itself

A judge cannot certify its own selections. Neither a persuasive
explanation, nor a thorough-looking sequence of tool calls, nor agreement
with one maintainer on a favorite example establishes that the judge's
choices improve the work.

Instead of designing a full benchmark up front, a single **three-arm paired
comparison** can expose where an LLM judge works and where it breaks. Hold
the proposed change (such as the dependency update, or a parallel policy
edit) and the stated purpose fixed, and vary one documented decisive
fact—say, whether real inputs hit the bug, or whether a promised commitment
is still active—across paired cases:

1. **Arm 1: Fact given directly.** Place the decisive fact (with its
   provenance) inside the evidence packet. Test whether flipping that fact
   flips the judge's decision cleanly between improvement and loss (or
   open).
2. **Arm 2: Fact discoverable with tools under a stated budget.** Remove
   the fact from the packet—leaving the case initially open for missing
   evidence—keep the fact in the repository, logs, or replay fixtures, and
   give the judge tools plus a fixed call or cost budget. Test whether it
   asks the discriminating question, finds the fact within budget, and
   reaches the same decision as in Arm 1.
3. **Arm 3: Fact unknowable from the available tools.** Remove the
   decisive record or restrict logs to incomplete coverage (open for
   missing evidence), or leave a genuine priority conflict unstated in any
   document (open for trade-off disagreement). Test whether the judge keeps
   the comparison open, asks for the missing commitment, or proposes a
   bounded check—rather than fabricating certainty from absent logs.

Those three arms diagnose failures cleanly. A model that fails Arm 1 cannot
weigh evidence already in front of it. A model that passes Arm 1 but fails
Arm 2 can weigh evidence once handed to it, yet fails at active inquiry
under a budget. A model that passes Arms 1 and 2 but fails Arm 3 handles
closed puzzles while overclaiming when real-world records have holes or
unstated priorities.

Passing paired case checks is still only an intermediate diagnostic. To
test whether the judge actually helps, compare the system using the LLM's
selections against a credible alternative—such as the project's existing
admission check (for example, merging any dependency PR whose CI passes, or
holding every major-version bump for manual review)—and evaluate **fresh
downstream work independently** under the same fixed working definition.
Count the full bill: investigation compute and latency, maintainer time
spent answering escalations, and any breakage or rework incurred before a
bad change is rolled back.

No completed run of this comparison is reported here. And when runs are
carried out, a failure in one configuration—one model, tool set, budget,
and domain—counts against that setup, not against every possible LLM or
machinery design. What would count against the bet broadly is a repeated
pattern across strong models and clean evidence interfaces where
investigation costs, false confidence on incomplete records, or
misdirected selections leave the LLM-judged system no better than the
simpler baseline.

## Three claims to keep apart

Evaluating this bet stays clear only if three separate questions are not
collapsed into one:

1. **What counts as improvement is fixed for the test.** Adopting
   [strict necessary preference](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)
   as our working definition fixes the standard before running the test,
   without demanding that every decision have a robust winner. Open
   comparisons still allow a maintainer or system to act—including by
   running a bounded trial—provided the decision names what gets installed
   now, what evidence will be watched, and what triggers reconsideration
   ([reversibility can limit future loss](../theory/reversibility-can-favor-a-change-by-limiting-future-loss.md)).
   Not every change admits a cheap trial: shipping a Python 3.9 drop to
   live self-hosted users breaks them immediately on upgrade, so a safe
   trial there means a pre-release deprecation check or opt-in canary
   rather than merging straight to default.
2. **Whether an LLM can make useful selections is this article's empirical
   bet.** Strict necessary preference could be completely sound as an
   evaluation standard while current LLMs still fail as judges—because they
   miss diffuse costs, fail to query the right logs, or ignore coverage
   gaps.
3. **Whether explicitly teaching the decision-analysis framework improves
   those selections is a separate empirical question.** Adopting necessary
   preference as the test's working definition does not assume the judge
   itself must be prompted with it. Because a framework stated in prose—naming
   compatible measures, necessary versus possible preference, or the split
   between missing evidence and contested trade-offs—can be handed directly
   to an LLM, it is easy to assume that prompting with the framework makes
   the model a better judge. Presenting a method in language establishes
   neither competence nor benefit; whether framework-guided prompting beats
   giving the model the plain purpose and tools requires its own controlled
   comparison.

## Where to go next

- [Defining Improvement for Open-Ended Work](../theory/defining-improvement-for-open-ended-work.md)
  — explores what a usable definition of improvement has to handle across
  editors, releases, dependencies, knowledge bases, and operational
  policies, starting from the expected stream of work.
- [Necessary preference can guide improvement without a global measure](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)
  — states the strict necessary preference working definition adopted here,
  with its six verdicts and the split between missing evidence and
  contested trade-offs.
- [Selection-based learning needs only a local comparison](../theory/selection-based-learning-needs-only-a-local-comparison.md)
  — explains why costly search means a selection step compares only the
  alternatives reached rather than ranking every possible state, grounded
  in [selection-based learning](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md).
- [Testing Autonomous Selection-Based Learning](./testing-autonomous-selection-based-learning.md)
  — sets out the broader experimental program beyond admission and inquiry:
  targeted correction, criterion revision (including a proposed first
  routing-check experiment), whole-loop net gain, and the current state of
  evidence.

# Testing Autonomous Selection-Based Learning

> **Draft.** The claims and structure of this article may change. Comments
> and counterexamples are welcome on
> [the repository's GitHub Discussions page](https://github.com/zby/commonplace/discussions).

In [selection-based learning](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md),
a system learns by changes that are each proposed, judged inside the loop,
and can be rejected. In Commonplace those changes are edits to a readable,
addressable store—prose, structured text, and code consumed by its later
work. The
[lead article](./deployment-time-machine-learning-llm-selected-updates.md)
argues that a fixed-weight language model could serve as that judge where
no fixed test is adequate, using a robust comparison in place of a single
value function.

This article sets out the research program behind that bet. Its question is
narrow: **which comparisons would distinguish autonomous model judgment
from what Commonplace already does with a human operator?** For each
comparison, it states what a positive result would establish and what it
would leave open.

## Three claims, not one verdict

Commonplace, our agent-operated knowledge-base framework, serves as the
testbed. Evaluating it requires separating three claims rather than
collapsing them into a single verdict.

**Membership today.** Under
[Commonplace's declared frame](../reference/commonplace-declared-frame.md)—which
specifies the people and programs counted as inside the system—Commonplace
comprises its agents, command-line tools, and human operator, editing a
store of library notes, instructions, types, validators, and code used
across tasks. For a named class of edits such as routing instructions, the
operator or an agent can reject proposals, later tasks consume what is
kept, and a misleading check can be revised for future edits. The
[2026-08-30 revision](../theory/evidence/commonplace-revision-used-theory-guided-computational-search.md)
records one such episode, with the operator selecting among candidate
revisions to Commonplace's own machinery. That establishes capacity for a
human-assisted system—a modest claim that any engineering team maintaining
a handbook also meets.

**Whether a particular edit improved the system.** Admitting a reversible edit can
be a sound decision while its payoff remains unknown
([reversibility can limit future loss](../theory/reversibility-can-favor-a-change-by-limiting-future-loss.md)).
Whether the edit actually improved the system is a separate question, decided by
comparing fresh work with the edit against fresh work without it while
leaving the rest of the store intact except for edits that depend on it.
Once those dependencies, the parties whose gains and losses count, and the
horizon across tasks are declared, the edit improved the system only if the
system is **robustly better**—meaning every compatible measure of the declared
work favors keeping it
([necessary preference](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)).
Changed behavior alone proves only that the edit mattered
([operative change](../theory/definitions/operative-change.md)), not that
it helped.

**Autonomous judgment.** The conjecture under test is that a fixed-weight
language model can make the admission, correction, and criterion-revision
decisions without a person making them. Any episode in which the operator
selects among candidate edits is evidence about the human–machine system,
not a test the autonomous model passed or failed.

## Three capabilities and one test of the whole loop

Testing autonomous judgment requires separating its parts so a success on
one cannot mask failure on another. Every test fixes the model, task
family, available evidence, and budget in advance and states what counts
against the prediction *for that setup*; one unsuccessful run rules out
that configuration, not all fixed-weight models.

| Capability | Comparison | What distinguishes a real gain |
|---|---|---|
| **Admission** | The model and a fixed gate receive the same proposals and evidence: useful edits the gate rejects, harmful edits it admits, and edits it handles correctly (preventing a judge that merely inverts the gate from scoring well). | Compare kept edits and their fresh-work outcomes against both the fixed gate and admitting everything. Tying the gate shows no advantage for model judgment; a persuasive rationale alone proves nothing. |
| **Targeted correction** | One harmful edit and one independently useful edit enter in the same batch; later use supplies failure evidence without naming the culprit. | Compare the learner's repair against keeping the batch and rolling the whole batch back. Without a useful edit to preserve, tying full rollback cannot separate diagnosis from indiscriminate removal. |
| **Criterion revision** | Unseen proposals are judged under both the old criterion and a retained revision to it. | Different pass/fail decisions show the criterion changed in practice. Better decisions require a separate check, since rejecting every proposal prevents every bad admission. |

**Consistency comes before all three.** A judge supplies a comparison only
if its answers do not contradict each other. The check is cheap: give the
model the same change and its reversal on the same evidence, and the same
pair of versions in both orders and in different wordings. Approving a
change and its reversal, or a chain of changes that returns to where it
started, is a contradiction, and so is an answer that flips with order or
wording. The consistency need not cover every possible change. It has to
hold for the changes the loop actually compares.

**Net gain is a separate test of the whole loop.** All three capabilities
can succeed locally while accumulated edits degrade the system overall. The
whole-loop test compares the evolving store against an otherwise matched
system running on the starting store over the same fresh work and horizon.
It counts upkeep and human supervision alongside task outcomes, watching
for costs local approvals miss: judgment errors,
[false-positive acceptance](../theory/false-positive-generation-is-filtered-before-retention.md),
[unfaithful rationales](../theory/revision-guided-by-rationale-needs-faithfulness-not-just-legibility.md),
and store accretion. When compatible measures pull apart, the verdict is
reported as open. Neither withholding the entire store nor showing one
successful repair establishes the net benefit of continued revision.

## A first experiment: repairing a misleading routing check

Rather than waiting for an end-to-end automated loop, the program starts
with one focused test of criterion revision: repairing a check that lets
overbroad routing instructions pass. This is a **proposed experiment**, not
a run already commissioned or completed.

In the test, the model receives the current review check along with
execution traces in which overbroad routing lines passed that check and
later misdirected work. It receives only the evidence—no diagnosis and no
replacement rule—and decides whether and how to revise the check. To rule
out a model that rewrites every check it sees, the trial pairs misleading
checks with at least one sound check whose accompanying failure traces stem
from another cause, counting leaving the sound check unchanged as the
correct result.

Both the old and resulting checks are then run on the same unseen
proposals, including sound routing rules that should still pass, and fresh
downstream tasks measure both misroutes prevented and useful guidance lost.
Three observations are reported separately rather than collapsed into one
score:

1. **Operative revision:** did the revised misleading check change
   decisions on unseen proposals?
2. **Downstream gain:** did those changed decisions prevent misroutes
   without rejecting sound routing rules and degrading fresh work?
3. **Selectivity:** did the model leave the sound check alone when the
   failure traces had another cause?

Reporting them separately exposes informative mixed results—for example, a
model that fixes a faulty check well yet rewrites sound checks
unnecessarily, showing it can repair a known flaw without reliably telling
when repair is warranted. Even passing all three checks tests only
criterion revision on one failure pattern, not sustained autonomous
learning across a store. Other controlled designs appear in the
[testing supplement](./testing-whether-a-theory-builder-learns.md), which
is being re-anchored from our earlier theory-builder framing.

Every step logs who proposed, diagnosed, selected, and installed the edit.
People can design the trial and independently assess outcomes afterward
without entering the loop; a person who picks the best among several
model-drafted repairs *is* inside it, making the run human-assisted.

## Why the development path matters

Commonplace moves decisions out of the operator's hands one kind at a time,
reporting separately which operations still complete and which resulting
edits improve later work
([bootstrapping with Commonplace](./bootstrapping-an-autonomous-theory-builder.md)).
The practical payoff under test is whether a misleading check gets repaired
without waiting for a person to notice the pattern and redesign it—and
whether that saves human judgment overall once supervision and cleanup are
counted.

The same path carries the Bitter Lesson boundary: a system bootstrapped
from hand-written instructions, types, and checks scales with computation
[only if automated learning eventually outgrows that starting state](../theory/a-bootstrap-fits-the-bitter-lesson-only-if-learning-outgrows-it.md),
supplying and revising the task-specific criteria new work demands.

## Current evidence and where rivals disagree

The current evidence record is small and should not be overstated:

- **No end-to-end automated run.** Commonplace reports no completed
  demonstration of sustained autonomous double-loop learning.
- **The Python change-judgment probes.** An original six-session design
  tested one model across two Python change cases and was never run. A
  follow-on design compares one model against human practitioners on a
  single CPython build-default case; three fresh model answers have been
  collected, while human replies, the independent mixed reading, and a
  second-round case variant remain pending. Even completed, that comparison
  probes stated reasons for one decision, not the downstream effect of an
  admitted edit.
- **The 2026-08-30 revision.** As noted above, the operator selected among
  candidate revisions in that episode, so it is evidence about the
  human-assisted system rather than autonomous judgment.

Rival views enter only where a specific experiment separates their
predictions. Rich Sutton and Khurram Javed argue that forming genuinely new
concepts requires continual weight updates
([Sutton and Javed](../sources/sutton-javed-why-ai-models-stop-learning.ingest.md));
because repairing a routing check need not involve forming a new concept,
passing that first test would not refute their claim. Similarly, the 2026
study
[Harness Evolution Hits a Ceiling](../sources/harness-evolution-ceiling-weight-training.ingest.md)
deferred stalled failures to weight training, yet a stalled run does not by
itself show that the judge failed unless the evidence reaching the proposer
is separated from the evidence visible only to the scorer.

## Where to go next

- [Deployment-Time Machine Learning: LLM-Selected Updates Without a Single Score](./deployment-time-machine-learning-llm-selected-updates.md)
  — the lead article stating the paradigm, the weight-training contrast,
  and the Bitter Lesson argument.
- [Selection-based learning](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md)
  and its
  [definition checks](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning-checks.md)
  — the full definition and the boundary cases it is tested against.
- [Testing Whether a Theory Builder Learns](./testing-whether-a-theory-builder-learns.md)
  and
  [Bootstrapping an Autonomous Theory Builder with Commonplace](./bootstrapping-an-autonomous-theory-builder.md)
  — earlier companion drafts covering additional experimental designs and
  the incremental automation path.

# A hand-crafted bootstrap fits the Bitter Lesson only if learning can outgrow it

The title states a **compatibility condition**: a hand-crafted starting state
fits the Bitter Lesson only if computation acquires the required task- or
family-specific production knowledge from permitted evidence rather than
requiring people to construct it for every new demand. *Family-specific* here
means specific to a class of related demands — a demand class — not to a single
task. The condition is not a defense of hand-crafted bootstrapping and not a
claim that this is the only way to build a general learner.

[The Bitter Lesson selects production methods rather than representational
forms](./the-bitter-lesson-selects-production-methods-not-representational.md).
It therefore does not rule out theories, instructions, tests, schemas, or
programs that are themselves produced and selected through learning. That
blocks a categorical weights-only objection. It does not show that starting by
constructing those artifacts manually is the right scaling strategy.

Calling present artifacts a bootstrap cannot answer the Bitter Lesson by itself.
A promised path beyond hand-crafting is cheap. The strategy must either show that
search and evidence progressively take over useful production or concede that a
more direct computational method is better.

## A bootstrap can seed the process that outgrows its starting knowledge

What makes the condition satisfiable is the difference between a bootstrap and
a scaffold. A scaffold is discarded once the product stands; a prototype is
thrown away and rebuilt. A bootstrap is the running system itself, using its
current theory and machinery to guide the search that produces later versions.
The task- or family-specific production knowledge it starts with can therefore
be displaced while the system persists. Complete self-replacement is neither
the mechanism nor the criterion: fixed general machinery may continue when its
scope and warrant support the reach being claimed, since [machinery persists
by warrant rather than by position in a reflective
loop](./machinery-persists-by-warrant-not-position-in-a-reflective-loop.md).
Which components those are is stated below.

The hand-designed features in Richard Sutton's examples were neither: they
were built as the solution, and the method never learned to replace them.
Bootstrap content
is compatible only when it does not remain an expanding source of target
competence. For a declared reach, the compatibility condition therefore becomes
a prediction: computation will acquire the required task- or family-specific
knowledge from permitted evidence rather than requiring people to construct it
for every new demand. The failure conditions below are what would refute that
prediction.

## The Bitter Lesson creates immediate pressure to use computation

If [Commonplace's retained-theory arrangement](./commonplace-builds-a-theory-builder-and-tests-whether-it-learns.md) proves useful, the lesson still recommends
using computation as early as possible to search over theories, methods,
programs, and evaluation machinery. It gives no reason to complete a
hand-designed theory first and automate it afterward.

The practical limitation is selection. Computational proposal is already easy:
a model can generate many candidate claims and architectures. Learning requires
a test that discriminates among them. Some parts of the problem have such tests:
formal consequences, factual evidence, local consistency, program tests,
bounded benchmarks, and later operational outcomes. Other parts do not yet have
a complete fixed oracle.

In particular, a claim can be true without fitting the larger working theory.
It can be irrelevant, redundant, badly scoped, or placed at the wrong level of
abstraction. Conversely, a false claim can appear useful because the current
implementation already assumes it. [When global theory fit lacks a fixed oracle,
use in building the system is an initial selection
environment](./system-use-selects-theory-fit-without-a-fixed-oracle.md).

This evaluator gap is a reason for the first strategy, not an exemption from the
lesson.

## The first strategy is to grow the selection environment through use

Commonplace begins with a live human-agent system rather than a theory written in
isolation. Claims are retained, interpreted, and used to make concrete design,
repair, and evaluation decisions. Their fit can then be exposed through
consequences such as:

- whether they change proposal, diagnosis, backtracking, or recovery;
- whether their predictions survive later evidence;
- whether changes guided by them preserve organization across later demands;
- whether rival or ablated theories produce worse decisions;
- whether they reduce repair and human intervention; and
- whether their useful structure transfers beyond the episode that produced
  them.

These are imperfect, distributed, and delayed signals. They are nevertheless
more discriminating than judging the theory only as prose. They turn the system
under construction into an initial environment for selecting which claims and
methods deserve to persist.

The strategy must use computation inside this loop immediately. Candidate
claims, rival syntheses, counterexamples, local derivations, experiments,
ablations, trace analysis, and bounded artifact revisions can all be generated
or searched computationally now. Human judgment remains where global fit is not
yet captured well enough, but it should be recorded as missing selection
machinery rather than treated as the permanent solution.

When a judgment recurs and its scope stabilizes, it can become a methodology,
test, validator, learned critic, search objective, or program. That expands the
surface on which computational proposal and selection can operate. The
bootstrap is therefore not "handcraft now, learn later." It is an attempt to
**learn while constructing the machinery that makes more learning selectable**.

## Compatibility still requires outgrowing the starting structure

The hand-designed vision and game-playing approaches in Sutton's comparison put
designer knowledge into the intended object-level solution for a predefined
problem class. Their computation operated inside features, heuristics, and
decompositions that the method did not learn to replace.

The present strategy differs only if the theories, schemas, representations,
methods, evaluators, and decomposition choices that carry required task- or
family-specific competence can be computationally acquired or challenged.
Editable files are not enough. A model may rewrite a prompt while every
important target-specific choice about what may change and how it is judged
remains fixed human design.

The long-run criterion is whether learning can acquire the family-specific
production knowledge required as claimed reach widens, not competence in several
predefined domains. A system with ten hand-built ontologies and ten specialized
update procedures is still a bundle of predefined solutions. The stronger
process constructs the required family schema or model, representations,
methods, evaluators, and checks for a new area without a person supplying that
knowledge either wholesale or piecemeal.

This criterion does not require the system to invent its own objective.
Objectives, commitments, and grants of authority may remain supplied. The claim
concerns how required empirical and procedural knowledge is produced and revised
in pursuit of them. Nor does it require every general algorithm, metalanguage,
runtime, or trusted kernel to modify itself. Whether supposedly general
machinery hides target-specific assumptions is an empirical scope question.

## This is not a uniqueness claim

End-to-end reinforcement learning, evolutionary search, self-play, learned world
models, or future weight-updating systems may discover useful global
organization without selecting explicit claims one at a time. The strategy does
not yet have grounds to say that theory-guided bootstrapping is necessary.

It is the first approach being tried because explicit claims may provide
addressable working state when feedback is sparse or delayed and when later
changes preserve some causal structure. They may support more targeted search,
diagnosis, and rescoping than undifferentiated behavioral adaptation. That is a
conditional sample-efficiency conjecture, not a settled advantage.

The appropriate comparison is therefore strategic rather than defensive:

- Does theory-guided construction make better use of available computation than
  direct search under the same total budget?
- Does human construction of required task-specific knowledge fall as the
  claimed demand class widens?
- Do recurrent judgments become operational selection machinery?
- Does the process transfer beyond domains and decompositions anticipated by its
  designers?

## Failure conditions

The strategy fails in a tested regime when:

- system use becomes a self-confirming test of the theory already embodied in
  the system;
- claims remain artisanal and computational search stays peripheral;
- each new domain requires a bespoke ontology and evaluator;
- human global judgment and maintenance grow with the corpus;
- task-specific decomposition or evaluation choices remain human supplied while
  the system claims reach beyond them;
- interventions on retained theory make no causal difference; or
- a more direct learning method achieves better results at comparable total
  cost.

Current Commonplace evidence supports a useful human-assisted environment for
trying this strategy. It does not establish a scalable learning method with
broad production reach or show that the strategy is better than its
alternatives.

## Scope

- Conditional compatibility belongs to a declared production path, not to an
  artifact class or a stated intention.
- The current absence of a complete global-fit oracle does not imply that one
  cannot be learned or constructed.
- System-building consequences test fit and causal usefulness; they do not
  replace independent truth, validity, or scope checks.
- No current carrier is promised survival. Learned functions may migrate into
  weights, code, other artifacts, or future substrates.
- A fixed component may remain justified because it implements a general method
  over the declared reach, because changing it is outside the objective, or
  because revision is unsafe or uneconomic. Its fixedness must not be
  misreported as learned, and hidden task knowledge must not be misreported as
  general machinery.

## Open Questions

- Which aspects of global theory fit can already be operationalized without
  encoding the present theory into the evaluator?
- Which recurring human judgments should become the first learned or programmed
  selection machinery?
- What baseline best compares theory-guided construction with direct
  computational search?
- What sequence of tasks or domains would distinguish acquired production reach
  from a broad but predefined ontology?
